script.opening: "Honestly, doc, I think my mum’s overreacting. I went down a couple of times on the pitch last season but it was a scorching day and I hadn’t drunk enough — happens to loads of lads. I’ve got an academy trial coming up and I really just need you to say I’m fine to play, because if a doctor starts poking around they’ll pull me from the squad and that’s my whole life gone. So… I’m fine, right?"

facts.text: If pressed past the minimising: both collapses happened DURING exertion (mid-match), one with palpitations ("heart going mad") immediately before going down, both with little/no typical faint warning. Not after standing in heat off the pitch — DURING running. This is exertional syncope: a major red flag.

Reluctantly: a cousin (father’s side) died suddenly in his sleep at 23, "heart thing, no one really explained it". An uncle has "a pacemaker young". This is a family history suggestive of an inherited arrhythmia/cardiomyopathy (HCM, long QT, Brugada, ARVC).

HIDDEN AGENDA — the minimising IS the agenda: football is his entire identity and route out; an academy trial is imminent. He is terrified that being investigated means being pulled from the squad and losing everything, so he is actively downplaying genuinely dangerous symptoms to get "signed off".
If reached gently: he’s actually frightened too — he KNOWS the cousin story, has wondered, but cannot afford for it to be real this close to his trial. Bravado over fear.

Officially: to be cleared to play immediately. Actually (and what he needs): to be kept ALIVE — exertional syncope with a family history of young sudden death is potentially life-threatening — handled in a way that takes his career and his fear seriously rather than just slamming a door.

ice.ideas: It was heat and dehydration, normal for footballers; he just needs a doctor to clear him to play.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror that investigation will end his football career/academy trial, driving active minimisation of dangerous symptoms; underneath, a real buried fear about the cousin who died at 23.
ice.expectations: To be "signed off" fit to play today. What he actually needs: recognition that exertional syncope + family history of young sudden death is a potential emergency requiring urgent cardiac work-up and temporary cessation of high-intensity sport.

cues: "It only happens when I play" — exertional syncope is a cardinal red flag; do NOT accept the heat/dehydration reframe.
A cousin who died suddenly at 23 + an uncle with a young pacemaker — inherited cardiac disease until proven otherwise.
"Just say I’m fine so my trial isn’t affected" — the pressure to clear him is exactly the trap; safety must override.

checkpoints.text: Recognises EXERTIONAL syncope as a cardinal red flag and refuses to accept the heat/dehydration reframe: syncope DURING exercise, ± preceding palpitations, is potentially life-threatening and demands urgent cardiac assessment — not reassurance

Elicits and weights the family history: young sudden cardiac death (cousin at 23) and a young relative with a pacemaker strongly suggest an inherited cardiac condition (HCM, long QT, Brugada, ARVC, catecholaminergic VT)

Arranges urgent appropriate work-up: 12-lead ECG promptly (today), and referral for specialist cardiovascular assessment WITHIN 24 HOURS (NICE CG109 and QS71: TLoC during exertion and a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 are each 24-hour criteria, and a normal ECG does not remove the need) — echo, exercise testing, rhythm monitoring, family screening via the inherited cardiac conditions service — and does NOT clear him to play

Gives clear, safety-critical advice to STOP high-intensity exertion/competitive sport until assessed — explaining honestly that the next exertional episode could be fatal — while acknowledging the enormity of that for him

Holds the professional line against the pressure to "sign him off": does not provide false clearance to protect his trial; documents clearly; communicates appropriately (with consent, and given he is 19) and involves his mother/support as he wishes
Does not collude with the minimising to keep him happy; names the danger plainly but compassionately, and reaches the fear beneath the bravado (the cousin)

Takes his career and identity seriously — frames assessment as protecting his future and his life, exploring how to support the trial situation honestly rather than dismissing what football means to him

Safety-nets emphatically: ECG today, specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours (NICE CG109), NO competitive/high-intensity sport meanwhile, no driving until assessed (exertional syncope is not a simple faint, so the DVLA reflex-syncope exemption does not apply), what to do if it happens again (and that bystanders should call 999/CPR), family-screening implications, and a defined urgent follow-up — a coordinated, life-protecting plan

worked.txt: "I hear you that it was hot and you were dehydrated — but I have to be really straight with you, because it matters more than your trial: the thing that worries me isn’t that you fainted, it’s WHEN. You went down while running, mid-match, one time with your heart racing first. Fainting DURING exercise is the one kind doctors never wave through, because of what it can mean."

"And what you told me about your cousin — dying suddenly in his sleep at 23 — plus an uncle with a pacemaker young: I can’t un-know that. Together with your collapses, it points to the possibility of an inherited heart-rhythm condition. These often hide in fit young athletes and announce themselves exactly like this."

"So I’m not going to do the thing you asked and sign you off, and I want to tell you why with total honesty, because you deserve that: if this is what I’m worried about, the next time you sprint for a ball it could stop your heart for good. I would never forgive myself for clearing you, and I don’t think you’d want me to once you really hear it."

"Can I say something? I think part of you has wondered about this since your cousin — and being this close to your trial, you couldn’t afford for it to be real. That’s completely human. But the bravest, most footballer thing you can do right now is get this checked, because a heart that’s sorted can often get back to sport safely — and an ignored one doesn’t get the chance."

"Here’s what happens now: an ECG today, and I’m referring you to a heart specialist to be seen within 24 hours — that’s the national rule for faints during exercise with a family history like yours — for a scan and rhythm tests; and because it can run in families, they’ll look at relatives too. Until you’ve been assessed, no competitive football, no flat-out training, and no driving. I know that’s the hardest sentence I could say to you. I’ll help you handle the trial situation honestly with the club— a real medical reason, managed properly, is not the end of your career."

"If you collapse again before the appointment, whoever’s with you calls 999 and starts CPR if you’re not responding — tell your mum and your mates that. I’ll chase the 24-hour cardiology assessment myself today and see you straight after. You came in wanting me to say you’re fine. I’m doing something better: I’m trying to make sure you get to be."

f.learning: Exertional syncope is a cardinal cardiac red flag — syncope DURING exercise, especially with preceding palpitations, is potentially life-threatening and must never be accepted as "heat and dehydration". Add a family history of young sudden cardiac death (a cousin at 23) and a young relative with a pacemaker, and the concern is an inherited cardiac condition (HCM, long QT, Brugada, ARVC, CPVT) that classically kills fit young athletes. The plan is urgent: ECG today, specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours (NICE CG109 and QS71 — exertional TLoC and a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 are each a 24-hour criterion; echo, exercise/rhythm testing, family screening), and — critically — STOP competitive/high-intensity sport and driving until assessed. The examinable hidden agenda is the minimising itself: football is his entire identity and an academy trial looms, so he actively downplays dangerous symptoms to be "signed off". The skill is to hold the professional line (no false clearance), refuse to collude, name the danger plainly but compassionately, reach the buried fear of the cousin, and take his career seriously by framing assessment as the route back to sport and to staying alive.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG109 (updated 2023) · NICE QS71 · ESC syncope guidelines (2018) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (updated September 2025) · GMC Confidentiality (2017)
knowledge.summary: Collapse during exercise is a cardinal cardiac red flag. With palpitations before one episode and a family history of sudden death at 23, he needs an ECG now and specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours, and must stop high-intensity sport until assessed.

points.t: Loss of consciousness during exercise, rather than after it, suggests a structural or arrhythmic cause. Palpitations immediately before collapse and little or no prodrome add to the concern. Heat and dehydration are a diagnosis of exclusion here, not a reassurance.

NICE CG109: refer within 24 hours for specialist cardiovascular assessment anyone with TLoC and any of: an ECG abnormality, heart failure, TLoC during exertion, a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 and/or an inherited cardiac condition, new or unexplained breathlessness, or a heart murmur. Deniz meets at least two criteria. NICE QS71 sets the same 24-hour standard.

NICE CG109: record a 12-lead ECG for everyone with TLoC. Look for QT prolongation, a Brugada pattern, pre-excitation, left ventricular hypertrophy or abnormal T waves. A normal ECG does not remove the need for the 24-hour referral when exertional syncope or the family history is present.

Inherited conditions that cause exertional collapse and sudden death in young athletes include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT and Brugada syndrome. An uncle with a pacemaker at a young age raises the possibility of inherited conduction disease.

Until specialist assessment, advise no competitive sport or high-intensity training. Ask relatives and teammates to call 999 and start CPR if he collapses and is unresponsive. The specialist, not the GP, decides return to play.

Sudden death of a young relative may prompt family screening through an inherited cardiac conditions service; the specialist decides which relatives to test. Syncope during exertion is not a simple faint, so the DVLA reflex-syncope exemption does not apply: advise him not to drive until assessed, and apply the DVLA standard for the cause found.

Exertional syncope with suspected inherited cardiac condition, explained in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Deniz, I’m Dr Lee. Your mum booked this, but I’d like to hear it from you. What’s been going on?
model.why: Addresses the adult patient directly and opens

model.text: Honestly, Mum’s overreacting. I went down a couple of times on the pitch, but it was boiling and I hadn’t drunk enough. Happens to loads of lads. I’ve got an academy trial coming up, so I just need you to say I’m fine.

I can hear how much the trial matters. I’ll be honest with you whatever I find, because I think that’s what you’d want. Can I ask about the two episodes properly, then tell you what I think and what we do next?
model.why: Acknowledges his goal without promising the outcome and sets the agenda

model.text: Go on.
Take me through the first one. What were you doing at the exact moment you went down?
model.why: Establishes whether syncope was during or after exertion

model.text: Chasing a ball down the wing, flat out. Next thing I’m on the grass with the physio over me.
Any warning at all? Feeling hot, sick, vision going grey?
Not really. Just gone.
And the second time?
model.why: Explores the second episode for palpitations

model.text: Mid-match again. My heart went mad, like really fast and thumping, then I went down. Came round quickly both times.
Any chest pain or breathlessness when you train, any jerking, tongue-biting or confusion afterwards?
model.why: Screens for structural heart symptoms and seizure features

model.text: No, nothing like that. No fits or anything.
Has anyone in your family died suddenly or young, or had heart problems or a pacemaker young?
model.why: Family history of sudden cardiac death and inherited cardiac disease

model.text: …My cousin, on Dad’s side. Died in his sleep at 23. A heart thing, nobody really explained. And my uncle’s had a pacemaker since he was young.
Thank you for telling me that. I noticed you paused before you said it. Has your cousin been on your mind with all this?
model.why: Follows the pause to the buried fear

model.text: Yeah. Course it has. But I can’t let it be that. Not now. Football’s everything. If a doctor starts poking around, they’ll pull me from the squad.
So you’ve been frightened about your heart, and more frightened that finding out will take football away?
Pretty much.

I respect you for being straight with me, so I’ll be straight back. What worries me isn’t that you fainted. It’s when. You went down while running flat out, once with your heart racing first, and with hardly any warning. Collapsing during exercise is the one kind of faint doctors never put down to heat.
model.why: Refuses the heat reframe and explains exertional syncope

model.text: It could still be the heat though.

It could, and I hope it is. But put together with your cousin and your uncle, it could be a heart rhythm condition that runs in families. They often show up exactly like this in fit young players. If that’s what it is, the next sprint could stop your heart. So I can’t sign you off today, and I don’t think you’d really want me to.
model.why: Weights the family history and holds the professional line honestly

model.text: So that’s it. Career over.

No. This is how you protect it. Many of these conditions can be treated, and some players get back to sport after specialist assessment. A heart that’s checked has a future in football. One that’s ignored may not get the chance.
model.why: Takes his career seriously and reframes assessment as the route back

model.text: Here’s the plan. I’d like you to come in today for a heart tracing. And I’m referring you to the heart specialists to be seen within 24 hours, for a scan of your heart and rhythm tests. Can you get here this afternoon?
model.why: Same-day ECG and specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours (NICE CG109)

model.text: Yeah, I can get a lift.

Good, and a lift is right: please don’t drive until you’ve been seen. Until the specialist clears you, no matches and no flat-out training. I know that’s the hardest thing I could say. What would help with the club?
model.why: Clear activity and driving advice, then invites his priorities

model.text: If I just go missing they’ll think I’m not bothered.

Nothing goes to the club without your say-so; you’re 19 and it’s your information. If you want, I can write a letter saying you’re under urgent medical assessment and can’t play for now, without details. A proper medical reason, handled well, isn’t the end of a career.
model.why: Respects confidentiality and offers practical help with the trial

model.text: Yeah. That would help.

If you collapse again, or get chest pain or your heart racing that doesn’t settle, anyone with you calls 999 straight away and starts CPR if you’re not responding. Please tell your mum and your teammates that. I’ll chase the appointment myself and ring you tomorrow.
model.why: Emphatic safety-net including bystander CPR and GP follow-up

model.text: Okay.
Would you like me to speak to your mum as well, or would you rather tell her yourself? And when you do, what will you tell her?
model.why: Consent for family involvement and teach-back

model.text: I’ll tell her. Heart test today, specialist tomorrow, no football till they say so, and if I go down again she rings 999. She’ll be relieved someone listened.
Exactly. You wanted me to say you’re fine. I’m trying to make sure you get to be.
model.why: Closes by linking the plan to his goal

social.t: Football is his identity, his route forward and possibly his income. Losing the trial feels like losing everything, which drives the minimising.
His mother booked the appointment. A cousin’s death and an uncle’s pacemaker on his father’s side mean the wider family may be affected; the specialist service advises on who to screen.

legal.t: Exertional syncope is not a simple faint, so the reflex-syncope exemption does not apply. Advise no driving until specialist assessment, then apply the DVLA standard for the cause found (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive, updated September 2025).

At 19 he is an adult. Share information with his mother or club only with his consent (GMC Confidentiality 2017). A letter to the club can confirm medical unfitness to play without giving clinical details.

professional.t: Signing him fit to play under pressure would be unsafe and dishonest (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). Document the history, the advice given and his understanding.
If he is paid to play, a fit note can state he is not fit for sport pending cardiology assessment.

community.t: Cardiac Risk in the Young (CRY) supports families after young sudden cardiac death; Arrhythmia Alliance for patient information; encourage family and teammates to learn CPR.

pitfalls.intro: This station is built around pressure to collude. It is failed by the candidate who accepts the heat story to keep him happy, and by the one who is right but so blunt that he walks away from the plan.

items.fail: Accepting heat and dehydration and advising fluids.
items.why: Exertional syncope is a NICE CG109 red flag; missing it can be fatal.
items.fix: Establish timing precisely: “What were you doing at the exact moment you went down?”

items.fail: Routine cardiology referral with no timescale.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE CG109 requires specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours.
items.fix: ECG today and a referral to be seen within 24 hours, with the GP chasing it.

items.fail: Not asking about family history, or asking only about parents.
items.why: The cousin’s sudden death at 23 and the uncle’s pacemaker are decisive and only come out if asked broadly.
items.fix: “Has anyone in the family died suddenly or young, or had a pacemaker or heart problem young?”

items.why: Overstated and crushing; he disengages and plays anyway.
items.fix: “No matches until the specialist has seen you. Many of these conditions can be treated, and this is how you protect your career.”

items.fail: Talking to his mother about the plan without asking him.
items.why: He is 19; it breaches confidentiality and undermines his autonomy.
items.fix: Ask whether he wants his mother involved, and how.

items.fail: Safety-netting with “come back if it happens again”.
items.why: A further episode may be cardiac arrest; he will not be the one to come back.
items.fix: Tell him and those around him: 999 and CPR if he collapses and is unresponsive.

Good, and a lift is right: please don’t drive until you’ve been seen. Until the specialist clears you, no matches and no flat-out training. I know that’s the hardest thing I could say. What would help with the club?
SCA_MODELS.why: Clear activity and driving advice, then invites his priorities

SCA_MODELS.text: If I just go missing they’ll think I’m not bothered.

Nothing goes to the club without your say-so; you’re 19 and it’s your information. If you want, I can write a letter saying you’re under urgent medical assessment and can’t play for now, without details. A proper medical reason, handled well, isn’t the end of a career.
SCA_MODELS.why: Respects confidentiality and offers practical help with the trial

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah. That would help.

If you collapse again, or get chest pain or your heart racing that doesn’t settle, anyone with you calls 999 straight away and starts CPR if you’re not responding. Please tell your mum and your teammates that. I’ll chase the appointment myself and ring you tomorrow.
SCA_MODELS.why: Emphatic safety-net including bystander CPR and GP follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
Would you like me to speak to your mum as well, or would you rather tell her yourself? And when you do, what will you tell her?
SCA_MODELS.why: Consent for family involvement and teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll tell her. Heart test today, specialist tomorrow, no football till they say so, and if I go down again she rings 999. She’ll be relieved someone listened.
Exactly. You wanted me to say you’re fine. I’m trying to make sure you get to be.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes by linking the plan to his goal

SCA_STEM.name: Deniz Aydin
SCA_STEM.recent: Two witnessed collapses during matches last season, both attributed to heat and dehydration at the time; not previously assessed. No ECG on record. Appointment booked by his mother.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation about collapses on the pitch. Wants to be “signed off” before an academy trial.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG109 (updated 2023) · NICE QS71 · ESC syncope guidelines (2018) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (updated September 2025) · GMC Confidentiality (2017)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Collapse during exercise is a cardinal cardiac red flag. With palpitations before one episode and a family history of sudden death at 23, he needs an ECG now and specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours, and must stop high-intensity sport until assessed.

points.t: Loss of consciousness during exercise, rather than after it, suggests a structural or arrhythmic cause. Palpitations immediately before collapse and little or no prodrome add to the concern. Heat and dehydration are a diagnosis of exclusion here, not a reassurance.

NICE CG109: refer within 24 hours for specialist cardiovascular assessment anyone with TLoC and any of: an ECG abnormality, heart failure, TLoC during exertion, a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 and/or an inherited cardiac condition, new or unexplained breathlessness, or a heart murmur. Deniz meets at least two criteria. NICE QS71 sets the same 24-hour standard.

NICE CG109: record a 12-lead ECG for everyone with TLoC. Look for QT prolongation, a Brugada pattern, pre-excitation, left ventricular hypertrophy or abnormal T waves. A normal ECG does not remove the need for the 24-hour referral when exertional syncope or the family history is present.

Inherited conditions that cause exertional collapse and sudden death in young athletes include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT and Brugada syndrome. An uncle with a pacemaker at a young age raises the possibility of inherited conduction disease.

Until specialist assessment, advise no competitive sport or high-intensity training. Ask relatives and teammates to call 999 and start CPR if he collapses and is unresponsive. The specialist, not the GP, decides return to play.

Sudden death of a young relative may prompt family screening through an inherited cardiac conditions service; the specialist decides which relatives to test. Syncope during exertion is not a simple faint, so the DVLA reflex-syncope exemption does not apply: advise him not to drive until assessed, and apply the DVLA standard for the cause found.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Addressed the 19-year-old directly; heard the request for sign-off without agreeing to it.
Football as identity and income, imminent academy trial, mother’s involvement, driving.
Picked up the pause before the family history and ‘they’ll pull me from the squad’, and explored both.
Idea (heat and dehydration), concern (losing football, and the buried fear about his cousin), expectation (to be signed off today).
12-lead ECG today; cardiovascular examination at the same visit; echo, exercise and rhythm testing via the specialist.
Inherited arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy vs reflex syncope vs seizure; timing, prodrome and palpitations used to discriminate.
Recognised exertional syncope, palpitations before collapse and family history of sudden death under 40 as NICE CG109 red flags.
Exertional syncope with suspected inherited cardiac condition, explained in plain words.
Specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours; no competitive sport or high-intensity training; no driving until assessed; no false clearance.
Club letter with his consent and without clinical detail; family screening implications raised; mother involved as he wishes.
999 and bystander CPR if he collapses; GP chases the referral and phones tomorrow.

social.t: Football is his identity, his route forward and possibly his income. Losing the trial feels like losing everything, which drives the minimising.
His mother booked the appointment. A cousin’s death and an uncle’s pacemaker on his father’s side mean the wider family may be affected; the specialist service advises on who to screen.

legal.t: Exertional syncope is not a simple faint, so the reflex-syncope exemption does not apply. Advise no driving until specialist assessment, then apply the DVLA standard for the cause found (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive, updated September 2025).

At 19 he is an adult. Share information with his mother or club only with his consent (GMC Confidentiality 2017). A letter to the club can confirm medical unfitness to play without giving clinical details.

professional.t: Signing him fit to play under pressure would be unsafe and dishonest (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). Document the history, the advice given and his understanding.
If he is paid to play, a fit note can state he is not fit for sport pending cardiology assessment.

community.t: Cardiac Risk in the Young (CRY) supports families after young sudden cardiac death; Arrhythmia Alliance for patient information; encourage family and teammates to learn CPR.

redFlags: Syncope during exertion, little or no prodrome, palpitations immediately before collapse
Family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 or inherited cardiac condition; young relative with a pacemaker
Any of these with TLoC: specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours (NICE CG109)
psychosocial: Football as identity and income; imminent academy trial
Mother’s involvement and his autonomy at 19
Buried fear after his cousin’s death
ice: Idea: “It was the heat and I hadn’t drunk enough.”
Concern: investigation will end his career; underneath, it might be what killed his cousin
Expectation: to be signed off fit to play today

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Recurrent exertional syncope, one episode preceded by palpitations, with a family history of sudden unexplained death at 23 and a young relative with a pacemaker: suspected inherited arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy until proven otherwise.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Fainting while you’re sprinting, with your heart racing first, can mean the heart’s rhythm is going wrong under strain. With what happened to your cousin, we need to check whether you have a heart condition that runs in families. Many can be treated, but only once we know.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been scared this is what happened to your cousin, and more scared that finding out ends football. Getting checked is how you protect both your life and your career.”
management.psychosocial: Confidential club letter with consent; involve his mother as he chooses; acknowledge the loss of the trial and offer follow-up support.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is built around pressure to collude. It is failed by the candidate who accepts the heat story to keep him happy, and by the one who is right but so blunt that he walks away from the plan.

items.fail: Accepting heat and dehydration and advising fluids.
items.why: Exertional syncope is a NICE CG109 red flag; missing it can be fatal.
items.fix: Establish timing precisely: “What were you doing at the exact moment you went down?”

items.fail: Routine cardiology referral with no timescale.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE CG109 requires specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours.
items.fix: ECG today and a referral to be seen within 24 hours, with the GP chasing it.

items.fail: Not asking about family history, or asking only about parents.
items.why: The cousin’s sudden death at 23 and the uncle’s pacemaker are decisive and only come out if asked broadly.
items.fix: “Has anyone in the family died suddenly or young, or had a pacemaker or heart problem young?”

items.why: Overstated and crushing; he disengages and plays anyway.
items.fix: “No matches until the specialist has seen you. Many of these conditions can be treated, and this is how you protect your career.”

items.fail: Talking to his mother about the plan without asking him.
items.why: He is 19; it breaches confidentiality and undermines his autonomy.
items.fix: Ask whether he wants his mother involved, and how.

items.fail: Safety-netting with “come back if it happens again”.
items.why: A further episode may be cardiac arrest; he will not be the one to come back.
items.fix: Tell him and those around him: 999 and CPR if he collapses and is unresponsive.
